stem: For which type of business is job costing most suitable?

options.content: One that produces to individual customers' orders
options.rationale: Correct: each order differs, so each is costed separately.

options.content: One that produces a single standard item continuously
options.rationale: That business uses unit costing.

options.content: One that buys and sells goods without changing them
options.rationale: Trading businesses use cost of sales, not job costs.

options.content: One whose costs are all fixed in the short run
options.rationale: Job costing is about tracing costs to orders, not behaviour.

explanation: Job costing traces costs to each customer's order. A business making one standard product uses unit costing.

stem: How is the cost per unit of a batch found?

options.content: Prime cost of the batch ÷ number of units sold
options.rationale: It leaves out overheads and uses units sold instead of units produced.

options.content: Total cost of the batch × number of units
options.rationale: This multiplies instead of dividing.

options.content: Selling price of the batch ÷ number of units
options.rationale: That gives the revenue per unit, not the cost.

options.content: Total cost of the batch ÷ number of units produced
options.rationale: Correct: the whole batch cost is shared by the units.

explanation: Cost per unit = total batch cost (prime cost plus absorbed overheads) ÷ units produced.

stem: What is the difference between a mark-up and a margin?

options.content: Mark-up is a percentage of selling price; margin is a percentage of cost
options.rationale: The wrong way round.

options.content: They are the same and are used in the same way
options.rationale: They give different selling prices for the same percentage.

options.content: Mark-up includes overheads and margin excludes them
options.rationale: Both are applied to a stated cost; neither is about overheads.

options.content: Mark-up is a percentage of cost; margin is a percentage of selling price
options.rationale: Correct: they use different bases.

explanation: Mark-up = profit ÷ cost. Margin = profit ÷ selling price. A 25% mark-up equals a 20% margin.

stem: The total cost of a job is US\$250. The firm adds a mark-up of 40% on cost. What is the selling price?

options.rationale: This is the profit only, not the price.
Correct: 250 × 1.40.
This divides by 0.6, treating 40% as a margin on the price.
This adds 40 as a dollar amount to the cost.

explanation: Selling price = 250 + 40% × 250 = US\$350.
hints: Mark-up is a percentage of cost.

stem: The total cost of a job is US\$200. The firm wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. What is the selling price?

options.rationale: This adds 20% of the cost, which is a mark-up and not a margin.
Correct: 200 ÷ 0.80.
This adds 10% to the cost.
This takes 20% off the cost instead of adding profit.

explanation: With a 20% margin, cost is 80% of the price: price = 200 ÷ 0.80 = US\$250 (a mark-up of 25%).
hints: Cost is 80% of the selling price.

stem: A batch has a set-up cost of US\$300. If the batch size doubles and the other costs per unit stay the same, what happens to the cost per unit?

options.content: It rises, because more units are made
options.rationale: Variable costs per unit are the same; only the set-up per unit changes.

options.content: It stays the same, because costs are proportional to output
options.rationale: The set-up cost is fixed for the batch.

options.content: It falls, because the set-up cost is shared by more units
options.rationale: Correct: the set-up per unit is halved.

options.content: It falls to zero because set-up is a fixed cost
options.rationale: It is spread over more units, not removed.

explanation: The set-up cost is incurred once per batch, so a bigger batch gives a lower set-up cost per unit.
hints: Divide the batch set-up cost by the number of units.

stem: A printer quotes all jobs at 10% above total cost. A rival says this wastes money. What is the best comment?

options.content: A fixed mark-up guarantees every job earns the same profit in dollars
options.rationale: A percentage gives different dollar profits for different costs.

options.content: Cost-plus pricing cannot be used for jobs, only for batches
options.rationale: It is used widely in job costing.

options.content: A fixed percentage ignores competition and may price some jobs too high or low
options.rationale: Correct: cost-plus pricing ignores the market.

options.content: Only the materials should be included in the cost
options.rationale: Labour and overheads should also be included.

explanation: Cost-plus pricing is simple and ensures that cost is covered, but it ignores demand and competitors' prices.

stem: A job cost sheet includes the overhead absorbed by the job at the pre-determined rate.
explanation: True. Production overhead is absorbed at the rate on the stated base, such as direct labour hours.

stem: A mark-up of 50% on cost gives a profit margin of 50% on selling price.
explanation: False. Cost 100 plus 50% gives 150; profit 50 is 33.3% of the price.
hints: Work out with a cost of 100.

stem: Match each business to the costing method most suitable.

left.content: A bakery producing 3,000 identical loaves in a run
A cement works making one grade of cement

right.content: Job costing in a service business

explanation: Individual orders: job costing. A run of identical items: batch costing. One standard product: unit costing. Repairs: job costing for a service.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses make up the {{blank:a}} cost. Adding absorbed production overhead gives the {{blank:b}} cost.

explanation: Prime cost plus production overhead is the production cost.

stem: Name the document on which the costs of an individual customer's order are recorded.
explanation: It is the job cost sheet (or job cost card).

stem: A Mutare joiner's job uses materials costing US\$380. A carpenter worked 14 hours at US\$6 an hour and a tool hired for the job cost US\$45. Calculate the prime cost of the job.
explanation: 380 + 14 × 6 + 45 = US\$509. Leaving out the hired tool gives US\$464.
workedSolution: 1. 380 + 14 × 6 + 45 = US\$509. Leaving out the hired tool gives US\$464.

stem: Production overhead is absorbed at US\$4.50 per direct labour hour. Using the previous question, calculate the production cost of the job.
explanation: Overhead absorbed = 14 × 4.5 = 63. Production cost = 509 + 63 = US\$572.

stem: The firm adds a mark-up of 30% to the production cost of US\$572. Calculate the selling price.
explanation: 572 × 1.30 = US\$743.60. Dividing by 0.70 would treat 30% as a margin on the price.
workedSolution: 1. 572 × 1.30 = US\$743.60. Dividing by 0.70 would treat 30% as a margin on the price.
hints: Mark-up is a percentage of cost.

stem: Instead, the firm wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price of the job costing US\$572. Calculate the selling price.
explanation: 572 ÷ 0.80 = US\$715. Adding 20% to the cost would give US\$686.40, which is a mark-up and not a margin.
workedSolution: 1. 572 ÷ 0.80 = US\$715. Adding 20% to the cost would give US\$686.40, which is a mark-up and not a margin.

stem: A Gweru factory makes a batch of 800 school bags. Materials cost US\$3,200; direct labour was 400 hours at US\$4; machine set-up for the batch cost US\$320; overhead is absorbed at US\$2.50 per labour hour. Calculate the cost of one bag to the nearest cent.
hints: Include the set-up and the overhead in the batch cost.

stem: Explain why a mark-up of 25% on cost is not the same as a margin of 25% on selling price.

points.description: A mark-up is calculated on cost and a margin on selling price
Profit is a smaller share of the larger price, so a 25% mark-up equals only a 20% margin

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The bases differ: mark-up uses cost and margin uses price. A 25% mark-up on cost 100 gives a price of 125 and a margin of 20%.

explanation: One mark for each point.

stem: Explain why a larger batch usually reduces the cost per unit.

points.description: Batch costs such as machine set-up are incurred once per batch
They are shared by more units in a larger batch
Other costs per unit stay the same, so the total cost per unit falls

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Costs like set-up are incurred once per batch, so a bigger batch shares them among more units. Other unit costs are unchanged, so the cost per unit falls.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Which cost is incurred once per batch?

stem: Evaluate the use of cost-plus pricing for jobs by a small signwriting business.

points.description: It is simple and ensures that each job covers its cost and a profit
It is based on a job cost sheet, which also helps to control costs
It ignores demand and competitors, so prices may be too high or too low
Judgement: useful as a starting point, adjusted for competitors' prices and the customer

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Cost-plus is simple and ensures that cost and profit are covered. But it ignores what customers will pay and what rivals charge. The signwriter should use it as a starting point and adjust for the market.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Give a use, a limit and a judgement.

stem: Gweru Signwriters produced a wooden sign. The job used timber US\$220, paint US\$65 and fixings US\$35. A carpenter worked 12 hours at US\$8 and a painter 5 hours at US\$7. Hire of a delivery vehicle for the job cost US\$60. Production overhead is absorbed at US\$5 per direct labour hour, and US\$74 of selling and administration overhead is charged to the job.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the prime cost of the job.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the production overhead absorbed by the job.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total cost of the job.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The business wants a profit margin of 20% on the selling price. Calculate the price to charge.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The customer offers US\$800 for the sign. Advise whether to accept, referring to your figures and one non-financial factor.

points.description: US\$800 is above the total cost of 670, so the job earns 130 profit
But the profit is below the target margin of 20% (the target price is higher)
Non-financial: the chance of repeat orders from the customer, or spare capacity; decide accordingly

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At US\$800 the job covers its cost of 670 with a profit of 130, but below the target margin. If the workshop has spare capacity and the customer may order again, accept; otherwise ask for more.

explanation: This item tests a job cost sheet, a margin-based price and a short recommendation.
hints: Direct labour hours for the overhead are carpenter plus painter.
Delivery hire is a direct expense.

stem: Bindura Cookies bakes cookies in batches. Each batch needs a machine set-up costing US\$200. All other costs (materials, labour and overhead) are US\$4 for each cookie. The business is deciding between a batch of 400 cookies and a batch of 1,000 cookies. The selling price is US\$5.50 a cookie.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the total cost of a batch of 400 cookies.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost per cookie in the small batch.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total cost of a batch of 1,000 cookies.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost per cookie in the large batch.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit on a large batch if all cookies are sold.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether the business should make the large batch.

points.description: The cost per cookie falls from US\$4.50 to US\$4.20 because the set-up is shared
The large batch earns more profit in total if all the cookies are sold
But demand may be below 1,000 cookies, leaving unsold stock that can go stale
Judgement: make the large batch if demand is reliable, otherwise make smaller batches more often

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The large batch cuts the cost per cookie and earns more if all are sold. However, unsold cookies would be wasted. It should be made only if demand is reliable.

hints: Compare cost per unit and the risk of unsold stock.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State two other examples of costs that are incurred once for each batch.

points.description: Quality inspection of the first items in the batch
Cleaning or changing tools between batches (or administration of the production order)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Inspection of the first items in a batch and cleaning the machine between batches.

parts.explanation: One mark for each valid example.

explanation: This item compares two batch sizes and evaluates the larger one.
hints: The set-up is incurred once per batch.
